forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Preston council forecasts return to surplus as reorganisation pause removes near-term funding pressure
news_drafts.lead: Preston City Council has no underlying structural deficit and expects to return to a general fund revenue surplus of £1.108m in 2028/29, according to its mid-year financial review. The council will balance its budget in 2026/27 and 2027/28 with planned support from reserves set aside for growth investments. The forecast improvement comes as the government's pause to local government reorganisation, announced on 7 September, removes a planned near-term funding call: the council had set aside £1m in earmarked reserves for reorganisation costs, with payments to Lancashire County Council now under review. The council continues to assume it will cease operations on 31 March 2028 and merge into a larger unitary authority from 1 April, but must now maintain financial flexibility while the government reviews the reorganisation process on an unknown timescale.
news_drafts.paper_title: Report to Council Financial Strategy Mid Year Review Sept 2026

news_drafts.headline: Preston gets clean audit bill but auditors warn council to plan for budget gap ahead
news_drafts.lead: Grant Thornton has issued an unqualified opinion on Preston's 2024/25 accounts, meaning the council's financial statements are without material concern. However, the external auditors have recommended the council develop savings plans to manage budget gaps identified in its Medium Term Financial Strategy, the three-to-five-year spending plan. The auditors specifically warn against relying on money set aside in reserves to cover the shortfall, citing the need for the council to remain financially sustainable. The council's Audit Committee received the recommendation at its meeting on 23 September.

news_drafts.headline: Preston council has 18 months to set its last budget before local authority merger
news_drafts.lead: Preston City Council will cease to exist on 1 April 2028, when a new unitary authority takes over running services in the area. The Cabinet has confirmed that the 2027/28 budget will very likely be the council's final financial plan. The council faces a statutory deadline of 10 March 2027 to set council tax, the annual local levy residents and businesses pay to fund local services. The timetable paper warns explicitly that missing this deadline would put the council "in breach of the statutory process" and create "a financial impact on the Council". Councillors have already built contingency dates into their schedule—5 March and 8–10 March—should the primary meeting need deferral. Once parliament approves the Structural Changes Order formally establishing the reorganisation, new spending and asset-transfer controls will come into force, though the council has yet to publish the detail of what those restrictions will mean.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2026-27 Mid Year Review September 2026 with appendix
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation process has been paused, removing planned transitional funding calls but creating medium-term uncertainty about council structure.
findings.detail: The council had set aside £1m in earmarked reserves for LGR costs with plans to pay Lancashire County Council £839,876 in quarterly instalments over two years. Following the pause of the LGR programme, this process is now under review. This removes a planned near-term funding call but creates uncertainty about eventual reorganisation costs and the council's future structure.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand major structural changes. The pause improves near-term cash position but eventual reorganisation could have significant implications for the council's standalone financial future.
findings.figures: £1m set aside in earmarked reserves; planned payments £839,876 over two years, now on hold
findings.quote: This process is currently under review as a result of the pause of Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2026-27 Mid Year Review September 2026 with appendix
findings.headline: Investment income exceeding forecast by £1.029m in 2026/27 due to higher bank rates and larger cash holdings, supporting deferral of external borrowing.
findings.detail: The council has benefited from the Bank of England maintaining bank rate at elevated levels. In-house investment income is forecast to increase by £660k for 2026/27, and external fund managers are delivering an additional £369k for 2026/27 and £183k for 2027/28. This additional £1.029m in 2026/27 treasury investment returns is contributing to the council's ability to defer external borrowing and maintain strong cash positions.
findings.matters: Strong treasury management delivering above-forecast returns provides a cash buffer, reduces reliance on external borrowing in the near term, and demonstrates competent financial management.
findings.figures: In-house investment income increase £660k; external fund managers increase £369k (2026/27); total treasury improvement 2026/27 £1.029m
findings.quote: Increase in investment income returns due interest rates set by the Bank of England remaining high and due to holding higher cash balances than forecast

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2026-27 Mid Year Review September 2026 with appendix
findings.headline: Business rates income growing with £1.9m additional growth in 2025/26 now flowing into 2026/27 forecast, and Collection Fund showing £4.394m accumulated surplus.
findings.detail: The council's business rates income is strengthening: 2025/26 outturn showed £1.9m growth, now included in the 2026/27 forecast. The Collection Fund for NNDR has an accumulated surplus of £4.394m as at 31 March 2026, of which the council's share is £1.758m. However, the council has written off a number of business rates debts due to business closures, indicating some collection risk in a post-pandemic economy.
findings.matters: Business rates growth improves the council's revenue base and forecast resilience. Collection fund surpluses provide a buffer, but write-offs suggest collection challenges remain.
findings.figures: Business rates growth 2025/26 £1.9m; Collection Fund NNDR surplus £4.394m; council's share £1.758m
findings.quote: In 2025/26 outturn, the Council reported business rates growth of £1.9m which has been included in this forecast

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy 2026-27 Mid Year Review September 2026 with appendix
findings.headline: Council has no underlying structural deficit and forecasts return to surplus from 2028/29, with general fund revenue surplus expected in those years.
findings.detail: The mid-year update shows the council in balance for 2026/27 and 2027/28 (with planned reserve support for growth investments), then forecasts surpluses of £1.108m in 2028/29 and £516k in 2029/30. Crucially, these are not weather-dependent variances but reflect structural improvement in the forecast position compared to March 2026.
findings.matters: The absence of structural deficit demonstrates the council's core revenues are sufficient to meet ongoing commitments without requiring emergency savings or service cuts.
findings.figures: 2026/27 balanced with £953k planned reserve call; 2028/29 surplus £1.108m; 2029/30 surplus £516k; 2029/30 call on reserves reverses to contribution of £516k
findings.quote: general fund revenue surplus is expected in 2028/29 and 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: - FINAL Appendix A - Audit Committee Annual Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: The council is facing reorganisation challenges while delivering major projects.
findings.detail: The Audit Committee, in its forward look for 2026/27, notes the importance of effective governance given the council's reorganisation challenges and major project delivery. The specific nature and financial impact of these challenges is not detailed in this report.
findings.matters: Council reorganisations typically involve operational and financial changes; unexplained challenges warrant monitoring by lenders assessing risk.
findings.quote: In looking forward to 2026/27 and beyond, given the reorganisation challenges facing the Council and the on-going delivery of major projects, the importance of an effective Audit Committee remains critical.
